title: The second of two
hook: the cave again: the second of two, do not grieve, Allah is with us (9:40)
carry: small, brave, ordinary things in the dark

segments.voice: Yesterday, bara'ah, the surah without bismillah, the one surah that opens with no words of mercy, and your line was the silence speaks. Did something missing say more than words would have? Day four hundred twenty-two.

Late in his life, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ calls for the march to Tabuk, in the worst of the heat. Some people find reasons to stay home. And at-Tawbah, verse thirty-eight, asks them: what's wrong with you, that when you're told to go out, you sink down heavily to the earth? Then, to people dragging their feet, the surah tells a story they all knew. You heard it on this path last year: the cave of Thawr, the night of the hijra, two men hiding while the searchers walked past. Today we come back to the cave, and look at who else was in the story.

Verse forty, in paraphrase: if you don't help him, God already helped him, when he was driven out, the second of two, when the two were in the cave, and he said to his companion, in Pickthall's words: "Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us." Then God sent down His sakina, His calm, on him. On whom? The verse just says him. Some commentators say the Prophet; others say Abu Bakr, the companion told not to grieve. The Arabic allows both, and commentators still discuss it. The verse's point, to the people staying home, is sharp: the Prophet doesn't need you. God helped him when he had one friend. But read the hijra in Bukhari, and the two in the cave weren't quite alone. Abu Bakr's son 'Abdullah came every night after dark, slept near the cave, and slipped back to Mecca before dawn to listen for news. A shepherd, 'Amir ibn Fuhayra, grazed sheep over their tracks and brought them milk. And Abu Bakr's daughter Asma', packing their food for the journey, found nothing to tie the bag with. So she tore her waistband in two and used it to tie up the provisions. She was called dhat an-nitaqayn, she of the two waistbands. The second of two is a phrase about friendship under pressure. Around the two in the cave were people who did small, brave, ordinary things in the dark. A torn belt. A night's walk. A flock driven over footprints.
screen: `IF YOU DON'T HELP, GOD ALREADY DID.` · `SAKINA SENT DOWN — ON WHOM?` · `A SON, A SHEPHERD, A DAUGHTER.` · `SHE OF THE TWO WAISTBANDS.` · then, large: `THE SECOND OF TWO.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone who stayed with you on a bad night: a hospital hallway, a long drive, a phone call that went past midnight. Then the people around that night you hardly thanked: the one who brought food, the one who drove, the one who covered for you at work. Hold them, one by one. If you pray, you can ask good for each of them by name. The bell holds the time.
Dhat an-nitaqayn, she of the two waistbands: Abu Bakr's daughter Asma', who tore her belt to tie up the Prophet's food for the hijra.
Your line: small, brave, ordinary things in the dark. Today, thank one person who helped you through something hard, especially if they did it quietly. Day four hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the night in the cave of Thawr with the story of the hijra, honoring the household of Abu Bakr who helped, and some comfort a frightened friend with the verse's words, la tahzan, inna Allaha ma'ana: do not grieve, God is with us.

original.note: Arabic: "the second of two," the Qur'an's phrase for the Prophet in the cave (9:40).

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about two men hiding.
what it means: a reminder to people hanging back that God helped the Prophet with one friend, and a household of quiet helpers around them.
what a scholar hears: the pronoun in 'sent down His sakina upon him' is disputed (the Prophet or Abu Bakr); Bukhari's hijra report names 'Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr, 'Amir ibn Fuhayra and Asma'.

sources.quoted: Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3905 (the hijra: 'Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr, 'Amir ibn Fuhayra, Asma' and her waistband)

notes: Pickthall wording of 9:40 ('Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us.') quoted from memory; please confirm exactly.
Year 1 day 95 covered the cave scene itself (two when God is the third; the spider and dove), so this day takes 9:38–40's context, the sakina pronoun, and the helpers named in Bukhari 3905.
Bukhari 3905 cited from memory for the details of 'Abdullah, 'Amir ibn Fuhayra and Asma's waistband; confirm (the waistband detail is also in Bukhari 2979).

Reports differ on how the two halves of Asma's waistband were used (one report: one tied the food, one the water skin; another: she tied the bag with one piece) and on whether the Prophet himself gave her the name; the script now says only that she tore it in two to tie up the provisions and was called dhat an-nitaqayn. Confirm.
